answer: An extracted dependency edge is traceable only when the edge record carries its provenance, not merely its endpoints. The book's provenance contract says a graph constructed from source references should record: (1) the source file/version or admitted document the edge came from; (2) the inference or extraction method and its date; (3) a confidence or evidence-status label; (4) edge freshness plus a deprecation/removal rule; and (5) named ownership of conflict resolution. Beyond those five fields, the inspected source identity, relation meaning and snapshot membership must be carried into the derived relationship, so an answer can be attributed to a specific snapshot (accept the historical answer only with its S1 attribution; reject or disclose a mixed-snapshot conclusion). The corroborating rationale is that neither the existence of an edge nor a successful traversal establishes current source support: source revision drift can invalidate an edge, an update should mark a relationship stale or unknown rather than treating absence of new inspection as proof of removal, and deleting a stale edge must not silently erase the historical reason it once existed. Conversely, an edge is not fact merely because a visualization draws it. Note the page's stated limit: this provenance contract is conceptual guidance, not a claim of an implemented graph service or an empirical benchmark.
